newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel not to blame for German woes, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Waigel not to blame for German woes, analysts say.

text.p: It was not supposed to turn out like this for German Finance Minister Theo Waigel.

Having recently started his ninth year in office, the easy going minister had hoped to be toasting a sweeping reform of Germany's tax system and taking his place as one of the architects of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Instead, Waigel has seen his tax plans frustrated at every turn and monetary union has left the government split and facing the likelihood of an embarrassing climbdown if Germany is unable to get its financial house in order.

The record of recent months has provided the press and opposition parties with plenty of critical fodder, but analysts offer a sympathetic assessment of the finance minister, saying fate has dealt him few winning hands.
"He is caught between a rock and a hard place," said Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London. "He is under lots of pressure."

She and others said that while Waigel might be a lightning rod for many of Germany's current economic woes, the 58-year-old Bavarian has become a hostage of sorts to the very economy he helps oversee and deep divisions within his own coalition that limit room for tackling the nation's problems head on.

At stake for Waigel is the credibility of German financial policy in the crucial countdown in monetary union, and closer to home, the fate of the ruling coalition with Chancellor Helmut Kohl facing a general election in September 1998.
The crux of Waigel's problems has been an economic landscape dominated by sluggish economic growth, high unemployment and strict criteria for joining monetary union.
"It makes for an awkward situation," said Holger Schmieding, senior economist at Merrill Lynich. "It would be difficult whoever was in the government."

The most recent example of Waigel's frustration came on Tuesday when the Bundestag lower house of parliament debated his plans to stimulate the economy with 30 billion marks ($16 billion) of cuts in income and corporate taxes.

Although the body agreed to press ahead with the plan, it has been rejected by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) who see it as favouring the rich and many doubt any comprehensive tax reform here will be realised by the turn of the century.

Economists said there was little wrong with the plan itself but that with national elections only 13 months away, it was amost inevitable that the SPD would use its control of the upper house of parliament to block Waigel's initiatives.
"In general, he is a poor chap. He can't push his ideas through because of parliamentary gridlock," said Stefan Schneider, economist at Paribas Capital Markets. "He has limited room for manoeuvre."
Analysts also sympathised with Waigel over his efforts to help Germany qualify for monetary union.

Although he has been criticised for failing to make larger strides toward cutting the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product as the Maastricht Treaty requries, economists said the real reason for Germany's deficit problems has been near-record high unemployment.

High joblessness increases government spending and cuts tax revenues, but is largely the result of structural rigidities in the labour market and cannot be reformed without a wide degree of consensus from unions, the government and employers.
"The government really lacks the teeth for this kind of reform," one analyst said.

Economists even granted Waigel some understanding for his often criticised comments that Germany will meet Maastricht Treaty deficit targets smack on the button and that he would not seek a looser interpretation of treaty rules.
Analysts point out the finance minister is under stiff political pressure to promise Germany will fully qualify for monetary union.

Edmund Stoiber, Bavarian state premier and a fellow member of Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) political party, has forced the government to promise strict adherence to the criteria by saying it would be better to delay monetary union, rather than to accept a weak euro.
"Stoiber is really breathing down his neck," Lifton said.

Maybe Waigel's worst sin, many said, was his handling of the now infamous revaluation of Germany's official assets at higher, market-determined levels, in hopes of winning a windfall profit for the government.
Whatever the merits of the plan, Waigel mishandled it, making a highly publicised visit to the Bundesbank to win its acceptance for the scheme.

The central bank, which is loath to appear under anyone's political thumb, sternly rejected the plan and forced Waigel to wait until 1998 for any profit transfer to take place -- too late to help Germany qualiy for EMU.
($ = 1.877 German Marks)
